flashcards.back: MD5 128-bit, SHA-1 160-bit, SHA-256 256-bit, SHA-512 512-bit. MD5 and SHA-1 are collision-broken. SHA-3 uses Keccak.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam tests which hashes are deprecated and their sizes.

flashcards.back: Hash the message, then encrypt the hash with the sender's private key. Verify with the public key. Provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, not confidentiality.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Frequently confused with encrypting for confidentiality.

flashcards.front: Encrypting for confidentiality with public keys
flashcards.back: Encrypt with the recipient's public key. Only the recipient's private key decrypts. Asymmetric is slow, so it exchanges a symmetric session key.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which key is used for confidentiality vs signing.

flashcards.back: CA issues certificates (X.509 v3); RA verifies identity; CRL and OCSP report revocation; a certificate binds a public key to an identity signed by the CA.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Questions ask which component performs which role.

flashcards.back: Split knowledge: no one person knows the whole secret. Dual control: two or more people must act together to perform a task.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Often paired and often confused in key management questions.

flashcards.back: ECB: identical blocks give identical ciphertext (weak). CBC chains blocks with an IV. CTR turns a block cipher into a stream cipher. GCM adds authentication.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam picks ECB as the insecure mode.

flashcards.back: Ciphertext-only; known-plaintext; chosen-plaintext (attacker picks plaintexts); chosen-ciphertext (attacker picks ciphertexts to decrypt).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Increasing attacker capability; questions give a scenario to classify.

flashcards.back: Use a unique random salt per password plus a slow key derivation function such as bcrypt, PBKDF2, scrypt, or Argon2.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Salted, slow hashing is the expected answer to password-storage attack questions.

flashcards.back: Birthday: a collision in an n-bit hash takes about 2^(n/2) tries. Meet-in-the-middle cut 2DES to about 2^57 effort, hence 3DES.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Explains why hashes need long outputs and why 2DES was skipped.

flashcards.back: Natural surveillance, natural access control, territorial reinforcement; maintenance supports all three.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Naming the three CPTED strategies is a common recall question.

flashcards.back: 3 to 4 feet deters casual trespassers. 6 to 7 feet is hard to climb. 8 feet with three strands of barbed wire deters determined intruders.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which height fits the threat.

flashcards.back: A ordinary combustibles, B flammable liquids, C energized electrical, D combustible metals, K cooking oils and fats.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Core recall; pairs with suppressant selection.

flashcards.back: A: water. B: CO2, foam, gas agents. C: CO2 or gas (non-conductive). D: dry powder. K: wet chemical.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Using water on electrical or metal fires is a classic wrong answer.

flashcards.back: Wet pipe: water always in pipes. Dry pipe: air in pipes. Pre-action: detection plus fused head, preferred for data centers. Deluge: open heads flood on detection.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Pre-action vs dry pipe distinction is commonly tested.

flashcards.back: Halon 1301 depletes ozone and was banned by the Montreal Protocol. Replacements include FM-200 (HFC-227ea), Inergen, and Novec 1230.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Appears as which agent is no longer permitted.

flashcards.back: About 64 to 75 degrees F (18 to 24 C) and 40 to 60 percent humidity. Low humidity causes static, high causes corrosion and condensation. Keep positive air pressure.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Numbers and effects are tested.

flashcards.back: Fault: momentary loss. Blackout: prolonged loss. Sag: momentary low. Brownout: prolonged low. Spike: momentary high. Surge: prolonged high.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam gives a description and asks the term.

flashcards.back: Clear: logical overwrite. Purge: degauss, cryptographic erase; defeats lab recovery. Destroy: shred, disintegrate, incinerate. Follows NIST SP 800-88.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Match method to data sensitivity and reuse.

flashcards.back: Certification: technical evaluation of controls. Accreditation (authorization to operate): management's formal acceptance of residual risk.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Management owns the risk acceptance decision.

flashcards.back: Initiation, development or acquisition, implementation and assessment, operations and maintenance, disposal.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Order and the point at which security enters each phase.

flashcards.back: 1 Physical, 2 Data Link, 3 Network, 4 Transport, 5 Session, 6 Presentation, 7 Application (Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Many questions give a layer number or name and expect the other.

flashcards.front: PDU name at each OSI layer (1 to 4, and 5 to 7)
flashcards.back: 1 bits, 2 frame, 3 packet, 4 segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP), 5-7 data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exams ask which PDU a device or attack works on.

flashcards.front: Data Link layer sublayers and addressing
flashcards.back: LLC (Logical Link Control) on top, MAC (Media Access Control) below. Uses 48-bit MAC addresses; switches and bridges operate here.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Switch vs router vs hub questions rely on this.

flashcards.back: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, sequenced, three-way handshake. UDP: connectionless, best-effort, low overhead (DNS, VoIP media, streaming).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Frequently tested distinction at Layer 4.

flashcards.back: SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK. A SYN flood leaves connections half-open to exhaust server resources.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Links the handshake to SYN flood DoS questions.

flashcards.front: TCP/IP model layers and OSI mapping
flashcards.back: Four layers: Link (OSI 1-2), Internet (OSI 3), Transport (OSI 4), Application (OSI 5-7).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam may ask where a protocol sits in the TCP/IP model.

flashcards.back: FTP 20 (data) and 21 (control); SSH 22; Telnet 23 (clear text).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Port and clear-text vs encrypted questions are common.

flashcards.back: SMTP 25 (587 submission), POP3 110 (995 with TLS), IMAP 143 (993 with TLS).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Email protocol ports and secure variants appear regularly.

flashcards.back: DNS 53 (UDP queries, TCP for zone transfers); DHCP UDP 67 server and 68 client; SNMP UDP 161 and traps 162.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Zone transfer on TCP 53 is a common trap.

flashcards.front: Ports: HTTP, HTTPS, LDAP, LDAPS, RDP
flashcards.back: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, LDAP 389, LDAPS 636, RDP 3389.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Secure vs insecure port pairs show up in scenario questions.

flashcards.back: 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal; no broadcast (uses multicast/anycast). IPsec support was originally mandatory but is now only recommended (RFC 6434).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Differences from IPv4 (32-bit) are tested.

flashcards.back: Policy decision point (policy engine plus policy administrator) decides; policy enforcement point enforces. Assume breach; no implicit trust from network location.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Defines the vocabulary used for zero trust questions.

flashcards.back: Control plane (decisions, centralised in the controller) is separated from the data plane (forwarding). Controllers talk southbound to devices (e.g. OpenFlow) and northbound to apps.
flashcards.whyItMatters: SDN architecture and its controller risk are examinable.

flashcards.back: IEEE 802.1Q tags frames to create logical Layer 2 segments; inter-VLAN traffic needs a Layer 3 device. Mitigate VLAN hopping with unused native VLAN and no DTP.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Segmentation and VLAN attack mitigations are exam favourites.

flashcards.back: Common order: 1 packet filter, 2 stateful inspection, 3 application-layer proxy, 4 dynamic packet filter, 5 kernel proxy (some texts put the proxy before stateful). NGFW adds app awareness, IPS, identity.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which generation or layer a firewall type works at.

flashcards.back: Circuit-level (e.g. SOCKS, around Layer 5) validates sessions without inspecting content; application proxy (Layer 7) inspects content per protocol.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishing proxies by layer is tested.

flashcards.front: IDS/IPS types by location and method
flashcards.back: NIDS watches network segments; HIDS watches a single host. Methods: signature-based (known), anomaly/behaviour-based (unknown, more false positives).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Placement and detection method questions are common.

flashcards.back: Forward proxy fronts clients going out to the internet; reverse proxy fronts servers receiving inbound requests (hides servers, TLS termination, caching).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Direction of protection is the usual trap.

flashcards.back: Honeypot: decoy system. Honeynet: network of honeypots. Darknet: unused address space that should receive no legitimate traffic. Beware enticement vs entrapment.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Deception tools appear with legal considerations.

flashcards.back: Supplicant (client), authenticator (switch/AP), authentication server (usually RADIUS). Port-based network access control.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Needed to answer NAC and enterprise Wi-Fi questions.

flashcards.back: EAP-TLS: client and server certificates. PEAP and EAP-TTLS: server certificate, tunnel carries client credentials. LEAP: weak, Cisco proprietary. EAP-FAST: PAC-based.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Which EAP method is strongest or needs a client PKI is common.

flashcards.back: WEP: RC4 with 24-bit IV, broken. WPA: TKIP/RC4. WPA2: AES-CCMP. WPA3: SAE handshake, forward secrecy, 192-bit enterprise suite.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Choosing the most secure wireless standard is tested.

flashcards.back: Evil twin (fake AP with same SSID), rogue AP (unauthorised AP on the network), deauthentication attack, WPS PIN brute force, war driving.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Rogue vs evil twin wording is exam material.

flashcards.back: Bluejacking: sending unsolicited messages. Bluesnarfing: stealing data. Bluebugging: taking control of the device.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishing the three is a classic question.

flashcards.front: Hub vs bridge vs switch vs router
flashcards.back: Hub (L1, repeats), bridge/switch (L2, MAC), router and Layer 3 switch (L3, IP), gateway (can translate across protocol layers).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Device-to-layer mapping appears constantly.

flashcards.back: NAC checks device health (patches, AV, config) before granting access and can quarantine failures into a remediation VLAN.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Endpoint compliance scenarios point to NAC.

flashcards.back: RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, encrypts only password. TACACS+: TCP 49, encrypts full payload, separates AAA. Diameter: successor to RADIUS, TCP/SCTP.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Protocol selection for AAA is tested.

flashcards.back: AH (IP protocol 51): integrity and authentication, no encryption. ESP (protocol 50): confidentiality plus optional integrity and authentication.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Core IPsec distinction.

flashcards.back: Transport: protects payload only, host-to-host. Tunnel: protects the whole original packet inside a new IP header, gateway-to-gateway.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Mode selection by use case is regularly tested.

flashcards.back: IKE uses UDP 500; NAT traversal encapsulates ESP in UDP 4500. AH breaks under NAT because it covers the IP header.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Explains AH vs NAT scenarios.

flashcards.back: PPTP: TCP 1723, weak. L2TP: UDP 1701, no encryption by itself, used with IPsec. L2F: Cisco, predecessor to L2TP.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Identifying weak or unencrypted tunnelling protocols.

flashcards.back: TLS succeeded SSL (SSL 2.0/3.0 deprecated). Handshake uses asymmetric cryptography/key agreement, then a symmetric session key. TLS 1.3 removes legacy ciphers and mandates forward secrecy.
flashcards.whyItMatters: TLS versions and key usage are heavily tested.

flashcards.back: SPF: authorised sending IPs (envelope sender). DKIM: digital signature verified via DNS public key. DMARC: policy (none/quarantine/reject), alignment and reporting. All use DNS TXT records.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Email authentication trio is a modern exam topic.

flashcards.back: S/MIME: hierarchical PKI with X.509 certificates. PGP: web of trust. Both provide message signing and encryption.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Trust model difference is tested.

flashcards.back: SIP signalling UDP/TCP 5060 (TLS 5061); RTP carries media; SRTP encrypts it. Threats: eavesdropping, vishing, SPIT, toll fraud.
flashcards.whyItMatters: VoIP control selection questions appear.

flashcards.back: Adds digital signatures to DNS records for origin authentication and integrity; it does NOT encrypt queries or provide confidentiality.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishes integrity from confidentiality in DNS.

flashcards.front: Remote access: split vs full tunnel
flashcards.back: Split tunnel sends only corporate traffic through the VPN (internet bypasses inspection, risk of pivoting). Full tunnel sends everything through the VPN.
flashcards.whyItMatters: VPN configuration risk questions.

flashcards.back: MPLS labels packets for fast forwarding between sites, sits between L2 and L3. Site-to-site VPN links networks; remote-access VPN links users.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Wide area connectivity and VPN types.

flashcards.front: CPTED stands for and aims to do what?
flashcards.back: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design: shape the physical environment (lighting, sightlines, natural access control, territorial reinforcement) to deter crime.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam links CPTED to natural surveillance and territoriality.

flashcards.back: Tailgating: following an authorized person without their knowledge. Piggybacking: entering with the authorized person's knowledge or consent. Mantraps/turnstiles counter both.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Tests the precise distinction and the mantrap countermeasure.

flashcards.back: About 3-4 ft deters casual trespassers; 6-7 ft is hard to climb easily; 8 ft topped with barbed wire deters determined intruders.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Numeric fence heights appear in physical security questions.

flashcards.back: Fail-safe: unlocks on power loss to protect life safety. Fail-secure: stays locked on power loss to protect assets. Life safety takes priority.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which to choose for egress doors.

flashcards.front: Preferred lock type for high-security areas needing audit and revocation
flashcards.back: Electronic or smart-card locks with logging, since credentials can be revoked and use is auditable, unlike mechanical keys.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Ties physical access to accountability.

flashcards.back: Something you know, something you have, something you are. Somewhere you are and something you do are often added as contextual factors.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Basic but exam requires correct classification of examples.

flashcards.front: Type I vs Type II biometric errors
flashcards.back: Type I = False Rejection Rate (FRR, valid user denied). Type II = False Acceptance Rate (FAR, impostor accepted). Type II is the security risk.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Mix-ups between Type I and II are a classic trap.

flashcards.back: The point where FAR equals FRR. Lower CER means a more accurate biometric; use it to compare products.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which metric to compare biometric devices.

flashcards.front: Most accepted vs most accurate biometrics (rule of thumb)
flashcards.back: Fingerprint and voice are widely accepted and cheap. Iris is highly accurate. Retina scans are accurate but intrusive and least accepted.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Questions ask for the best fit by accuracy versus user acceptance.

flashcards.back: Synchronous tokens use time or counter synchronization with the server (TOTP/HOTP). Asynchronous (challenge-response) tokens sign a server-supplied nonce.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam tests how OTP tokens generate codes.

flashcards.back: A unique random value added per password before hashing defeats precomputed rainbow tables and prevents identical passwords producing identical hashes.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Common question on protecting stored credentials.

flashcards.back: Favor length and screening against breached lists; do not force periodic rotation or composition rules; require change only on evidence of compromise.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Modern guidance contradicts old policies.

flashcards.back: Principal (user), Identity Provider (authenticates, issues assertions), Service Provider (consumes assertions). Assertions are XML signed by the IdP.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks who issues versus who consumes.

flashcards.back: Resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server. Outputs scoped access tokens, not authentication.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Roles are tested as a mapping exercise.

flashcards.back: An ID token (JWT) with identity claims, a UserInfo endpoint, and standard scopes such as openid.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishes authentication from authorization.

flashcards.back: Organizations keep control of their own identities and exchange signed assertions or tokens, establishing trust through metadata and certificates rather than sharing passwords.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Principle behind cross-organization SSO.

flashcards.front: Format of SAML assertions vs OIDC tokens
flashcards.back: SAML uses XML; OIDC ID tokens are JSON Web Tokens (JWT). SAML suits enterprise web SSO; OIDC suits mobile and APIs.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam compares protocols by format and use case.

flashcards.back: Account created in the SP at first successful federated login using attributes from the assertion, avoiding pre-provisioning.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguish from JIT privileged access.

flashcards.front: Access control models: defining feature of each
flashcards.back: DAC: owner decides. MAC: system enforces labels and clearances. RBAC: permissions tied to roles. ABAC: policy over attributes. Rule-based: global rules for all subjects.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Core mapping exercise for the authorization domain.

flashcards.back: Simple security: no read up. Star property: no write down. Protects confidentiality.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Often paired with MAC questions.

flashcards.back: Simple integrity: no read down. Star integrity: no write up. Protects integrity.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Contrast with Bell-LaPadula.

flashcards.back: Need-to-know limits access to information required for the job; least privilege limits rights/permissions to the minimum necessary to perform tasks.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Two related but distinct principles.

flashcards.front: Separation of duties vs dual control
flashcards.back: SoD splits steps of a process among different people. Dual control requires two people to act together on a single step (such as two keys).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam distinguishes the two.

flashcards.front: Access control matrix: ACL vs capability list
flashcards.back: ACL is a column: list of subjects with rights on one object. Capability list is a row: rights a subject holds across objects.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Tests matrix orientation.

flashcards.back: Constrained interface limits functions shown to user. Content-dependent control decides by data value; context-dependent by circumstances like time or sequence.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Specialized authorization mechanisms are tested by name.

flashcards.back: Provisioning, review/recertification, modification on transfer, and deprovisioning. Joiner-mover-leaver describes the same flow.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam uses joiner-mover-leaver terminology.

flashcards.back: Movers (role changes) are the usual source of privilege creep; leavers' orphaned accounts are the usual source of unauthorized access.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Identifies where audits focus.

flashcards.back: Aggregation: combining multiple low-level rights into powerful access. Creep: accumulating rights over time after role changes.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Often confused by candidates.

flashcards.front: Who authorizes access: data owner vs custodian
flashcards.back: Data owner approves access and classifies data; custodian implements and maintains technical controls under the owner's direction.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Core ISC2 role distinction.

flashcards.back: Role mining discovers roles by analyzing existing permissions (bottom-up); role engineering designs them top-down from business functions. Top-down gives cleaner governance.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam covers how RBAC roles are built.

flashcards.back: System for Cross-domain Identity Management: standard REST/JSON protocol to automate user provisioning and deprovisioning between identity provider and applications.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Named standard for automated lifecycle management.

flashcards.back: Kerberos KDC = Authentication Service + Ticket Granting Service; client gets a TGT, then service tickets. Symmetric keys, timestamps, default 5-minute clock-skew tolerance.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Frequently tested flow detail.

flashcards.back: Kerberos weaknesses: KDC is a single point of failure/compromise, clocks must be synchronized, replay is possible within ticket lifetime, and tickets allow offline password guessing.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks about Kerberos limitations.

flashcards.back: RADIUS: UDP, encrypts only the password, combines authentication and authorization. TACACS+: TCP, encrypts whole payload, separates AAA functions (Cisco origin).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Standard comparison question.

flashcards.back: LDAP uses 389; LDAPS uses 636. Directories follow X.500 style hierarchy with DNs; LDAP queries identity data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Port numbers are fair game.

flashcards.back: Extensible Authentication Protocol is a framework (not a method) for authentication in 802.1X; methods include EAP-TLS (mutual certificates), PEAP and EAP-TTLS.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Tests which EAP method is strongest: EAP-TLS.

flashcards.back: Credential vaulting, session recording, just-in-time elevation, approval workflows and rotation of privileged secrets after use.
flashcards.whyItMatters: PAM vocabulary shows up in scenario answers.

flashcards.back: Unpredictable session IDs, timeouts on idle and absolute lifetime, regeneration at login, secure/HttpOnly cookies, invalidation on logout.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Session controls are tested as authorization risks.

flashcards.back: Planning, discovery, attack (with a loop back to discovery as new hosts are found), then reporting. Reporting is also produced throughout.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks for the correct order and that planning/authorization comes first.

flashcards.front: Black box vs gray box vs white box testing
flashcards.back: Black: no prior knowledge (outsider). Gray: partial knowledge or limited credentials (insider). White: full knowledge, design and source (also called crystal or full-knowledge).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Questions map attacker profile to test type.

flashcards.back: VA finds and ranks weaknesses without exploiting them. Pen test exploits and chains weaknesses to demonstrate real impact, under written authorization.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Classic distinction; exploitation requires authorization.

flashcards.back: Written agreement defining scope, targets, permitted techniques, test windows, emergency contacts, and data handling. Must be approved before testing starts.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Written authorization is the first-step answer for pen test scenarios.

flashcards.front: Red team, blue team, purple team
flashcards.back: Red emulates the adversary; blue defends and detects; purple is collaboration where red and blue share findings to improve defenses.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which team attacks, which defends, and what purple adds.

flashcards.front: Internal vs external vs third-party audit
flashcards.back: Internal: own staff, reports to audit committee. External: independent firm, highest independence for outside parties. Third-party: provider audited by an independent party, shared as reports (for example SOC).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam probes who is independent and for whom.

flashcards.front: Why risk should drive assessment strategy
flashcards.back: Frequency and depth of testing should reflect asset criticality, threat level, and prior findings, not a fixed calendar or budget alone.
flashcards.whyItMatters: When options offer budget, last year's schedule, or risk, the risk-driven answer wins.

flashcards.back: SAST: analyzes source or binaries at rest, no execution. DAST: tests the running app from outside, no source needed. IAST: instrumented agent observes the app from inside while it is tested.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which method fits access to code or runtime.

flashcards.back: Supplies malformed, random, or unexpected input to a program to trigger crashes and expose flaws such as buffer overflows. Types: mutation-based (alters valid input) and generation-based (builds input from a model).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Know both what fuzzing finds and its two styles.

flashcards.front: Synthetic transactions vs real user monitoring
flashcards.back: Synthetic: scripted, repeatable simulated transactions run proactively (active). RUM: passive capture of actual user sessions.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Common pairing; active vs passive.

flashcards.back: Credentialed scans log in to inspect patches and configuration, giving fewer false positives and more depth. Non-credentialed shows what an external attacker sees.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Reducing false positives is a frequent scenario.

flashcards.back: False positive: reported flaw that does not exist. False negative: real flaw that the tool missed. False negatives are generally more dangerous.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam tests the terms and the greater risk.

flashcards.back: Measures the share of code, branches, functions, or requirements exercised by test cases. Low coverage indicates untested areas.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks what low coverage implies about testing thoroughness, not about security posture.

flashcards.back: Models how a malicious actor might subvert a feature, then tests that controls resist it. The attacker's counterpart of a use case.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishes abuse cases from use cases.

flashcards.back: Examines interactions between components: APIs, UIs, and server interfaces, covering data exchange, error handling, and boundary conditions.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks what interface testing covers (APIs, UIs, server boundaries) versus code review.

flashcards.back: Automated, continuous emulation of attacker techniques to check whether controls detect or block them. Complements pen tests but is safer and repeatable.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks BAS purpose: continuous automated control validation, safer and more repeatable than a pen test.

flashcards.back: Re-running prior tests after a change to confirm existing functions and security controls still work and no new defects appeared.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Often asked after patching or code changes.

flashcards.back: KPI: how well a process performs against objectives. KRI: leading signal that exposure to risk is rising. Example KRI: growing patch backlog.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam separates performance from risk signals.

flashcards.back: Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM): ongoing awareness of security, vulnerabilities, and threats to support risk-based decisions.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Maps the standard number to the concept.

flashcards.back: Periodic checks of accounts for orphaned, dormant, excessive, or privileged access, plus recertification at role change and termination.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Frequently tested with privilege creep scenarios.

flashcards.back: Accumulation of access rights as a person changes roles without old rights being removed; violates least privilege. Fixed by recertification at role change.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Typical finding in access reviews.

flashcards.back: Senior management periodically reviews audit results, metrics, incidents, and changes to confirm the ISMS is suitable, adequate, and effective, and directs improvements.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Know who does it and why.

flashcards.back: Success logs are not proof. Evidence of recoverability comes from periodic test restores measured against RTO and RPO.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Tests the difference between activity and assurance.

flashcards.back: Activity metrics show completion. Behavior metrics (phishing click rate trend, reporting rate) show effectiveness.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Best-metric questions favour behavior outcomes.

flashcards.front: Steps to take with a scanner finding
flashcards.back: Validate (rule out false positives), assess risk in context, prioritize, remediate or accept formally, then retest to verify closure.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Ordering and the verification step.

flashcards.front: Reporting to executives vs technical teams
flashcards.back: Executives: business impact, risk posture, decisions needed, concise. Technical teams: reproduction steps, evidence, and remediation detail.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Audience tailoring is a classic question.

flashcards.back: When a fix is infeasible, record a formal exception approved by the risk owner, add compensating controls, and set a review date.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Tests proper handling of unfixable findings.

flashcards.back: The accountable business or risk owner decides, with full information. Security advises and documents; it does not accept risk for the business.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Manager-mindset staple.

flashcards.back: Report immediately through the agreed escalation path rather than waiting for the final report, especially when exploitable and exposed.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Appears in pen test conduct scenarios.

flashcards.back: SOC 1: controls relevant to customer financial reporting (ICFR). SOC 2: Trust Services Criteria, restricted use. SOC 3: summarized SOC 2 for general public use.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Most tested audit-report distinction.

flashcards.front: Type I vs Type II report
flashcards.back: Type I: design of controls at a point in time. Type II: design plus operating effectiveness over a period (commonly 6 to 12 months).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Type II gives stronger assurance.

flashcards.back: Security (common criteria, always included), availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which criterion is mandatory in every SOC 2 (security) and to list the five.

flashcards.back: Controls the service provider assumes the customer implements; the customer must map them to its own environment.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks who must act on CUECs: the customer, not the provider.

flashcards.back: A subservice organization is excluded from the report scope, so its controls were not examined; the customer must seek separate assurance.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks why a carve-out leaves a gap the customer must close separately.

flashcards.back: Evidence obtained directly by the auditor (observation, re-performance, inspection) is more reliable than representations from the audited party.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Which evidence is MOST reliable.

flashcards.back: Auditors report to the audit committee or board, not to the function being audited, and should not audit controls they designed or operate.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Independence conflict scenarios.

flashcards.back: Plan (objectives, scope, criteria), perform fieldwork and collect evidence, analyze, report findings, then follow up on remediation.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Ordering question and planning first.

flashcards.back: Contract term letting a customer or its auditors examine a provider's controls. Accountability for the data stays with the customer regardless of outsourcing.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Third-party assurance and due diligence.

flashcards.front: Order of volatility (collect first to last)
flashcards.back: CPU registers/cache, RAM, network state and processes, disk, remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which evidence to gather first from a live system.

flashcards.front: Chain of custody records which facts?
flashcards.back: Who collected and handled the evidence, when, where, why and how it was stored or transferred, with each hand-off documented.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Gaps in custody are the classic reason evidence becomes inadmissible.

flashcards.front: Standard of proof: civil vs criminal
flashcards.back: Civil: preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Criminal: beyond a reasonable doubt.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Scenario questions test which burden an investigation must meet.

flashcards.back: A baseline threshold of acceptable errors (such as 3 failed logins) below which no alert is raised; crossing it triggers review.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Appears in questions on reducing monitoring noise.

flashcards.front: How should logs be protected from tampering?
flashcards.back: Send them to a central, access-restricted server in real time, use write-once storage and hashing, and synchronise clocks (NTP).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam favours centralised, protected logs for integrity and admissibility.

flashcards.back: Identification, change control, configuration status accounting, then verification and audit, all against a baseline.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Tests the sequence and difference from change management.

flashcards.back: Baseline is the approved secure standard; drift is any unapproved deviation from it, detected by comparison and corrected under change control.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Drift scenarios ask for automated detection plus change control.

flashcards.front: Separation of duties vs dual control vs split knowledge
flashcards.back: SoD divides a task among people; dual control needs two people to act together; split knowledge gives each only part of a secret.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Commonly confused trio on the exam.

flashcards.front: Job rotation and mandatory vacation purpose
flashcards.back: Both are detective controls that expose fraud and reduce reliance on one person by having others perform the duties.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which control detects collusion or fraud.

flashcards.back: Clear (logical overwrite), Purge (stronger, such as crypto erase or degauss), Destroy (physical destruction).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Know which method fits sensitivity and reuse of media.

flashcards.front: Why does degaussing not work on SSDs?
flashcards.back: Degaussing disrupts magnetic media; SSDs use flash. Use crypto erase, secure erase or destruction instead.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam traps pair SSDs with degaussing or overwriting.

flashcards.front: ISC2 incident management phases in order
flashcards.back: Detection, response, mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation, lessons learned.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Ordering questions expect this exact sequence.

flashcards.back: Recovery restores systems to normal operation; remediation fixes root causes and the vulnerability so the incident cannot recur.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Frequently confused phases in scenarios.

flashcards.back: Contain the incident and limit its scope and damage, for example by isolating hosts or disabling accounts.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishes containment from recovery and remediation.

flashcards.back: An event is any observable occurrence; an incident is an event that actually or potentially violates policy or harms confidentiality, integrity or availability.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam tests triage: first decide whether an event is an incident.

flashcards.back: Signature-based (known patterns), anomaly or behaviour-based (deviation from baseline), and heuristic or rule-based approaches.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Know the strengths: signatures miss zero-days, anomaly gives false positives.

flashcards.back: Enticement makes a target attractive to those already inclined; entrapment induces someone to commit a crime and may block prosecution.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Honeypot legality question.

flashcards.back: Scored 0 to 10: None 0, Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Used in prioritising vulnerabilities, but context also matters.

flashcards.back: Identify and assess, prioritise by risk, test, approve via change management, deploy, verify, and document with rollback ready.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam wants testing and change control before production deployment.

flashcards.back: Request, impact and security assessment, approval by CAB, build and test, schedule and implement with rollback plan, verify, document.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Ordering questions on change control.

flashcards.back: Expedite the fix, but document and review it afterward through the normal change process.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam rejects both skipping documentation and refusing the fix.

flashcards.back: Hot: ready with current data, minutes to hours. Warm: hardware, no current data, days. Cold: space and utilities only, weeks. Mobile: transportable unit.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Match site type to RTO and cost.

flashcards.back: RPO: acceptable data loss. RTO: time to restore. WRT: time to verify afterward. MTD: absolute limit; RTO + WRT must not exceed MTD.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Core recovery metrics with a frequently tested relationship.

flashcards.back: Full copies all; incremental copies changes since the last backup of any type (needs full plus all incrementals); differential copies changes since last full (needs full plus latest).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Calculation-style restore scenarios.

flashcards.back: 0: striping, no redundancy. 1: mirroring. 5: striping with parity, survives one disk loss. 10: striped mirrors (mirrored pairs, then striped).
flashcards.whyItMatters: Know which levels give redundancy; RAID is not a backup.

flashcards.back: BCP keeps critical business processes running during disruption; DRP is the IT-focused subset that restores systems and data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Classic definition distinction.

flashcards.front: Order of returning to primary site after disaster
flashcards.back: Move the least critical systems back first and the most critical last, after the site is proven stable.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Counterintuitive point the exam likes.

flashcards.front: DR test types, least to most disruptive
flashcards.back: Read-through (checklist), walkthrough (tabletop), simulation, parallel, full interruption.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Ordering of test types is a regular question.

flashcards.back: Parallel runs processing at the alternate site while production continues; full interruption shuts down primary and fails over for real.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Know which test risks live operations.

flashcards.back: Tabletop is a talk-through of the plan by key staff; simulation acts out a disaster scenario with participants performing their roles.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Distinguishes two low-impact tests.

flashcards.back: Project scope and planning, business impact analysis, continuity planning (strategy and plan), approval and implementation, then testing and maintenance.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Sequence question: BIA comes right after scope.

flashcards.front: What a business impact analysis produces
flashcards.back: Critical functions and dependencies, impact over time, and MTD, RTO and RPO recovery priorities.
flashcards.whyItMatters: BIA drives recovery strategy choice.

flashcards.back: A: ordinary combustibles. B: flammable liquids. C: electrical. D: combustible metals. K: cooking oils.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Pairing class with correct suppression is common.

flashcards.back: Wet pipe: always charged. Dry pipe: air-filled until triggered. Pre-action: needs detection event plus heat, best for data centres. Deluge: all heads open.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Pre-action is the usual data-centre answer.

flashcards.back: About 3-4 ft deters casual trespass, 6-7 ft is hard to climb, and 8 ft with barbed wire deters determined intruders.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Numbers can be tested directly.

flashcards.back: Spike: brief high voltage. Surge: prolonged high voltage. Sag: brief low voltage. Brownout: prolonged low. Blackout: total loss. Fault: brief total loss.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Terms and UPS or surge protector answers.

flashcards.back: A covert code or alarm signal an employee uses to tell security they are under coercion while appearing to comply.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Personnel safety control tested in scenarios.

flashcards.front: Priority in any conflict between safety and assets
flashcards.back: Human life and safety take priority over data, equipment and systems.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam answer when safety conflicts with recovery or evidence.

flashcards.front: CMMI maturity levels 1 to 5, in order
flashcards.back: 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitatively Managed, 5 Optimizing.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam gives a description (e.g. statistical control) and asks for the level.

flashcards.front: Waterfall vs spiral: which is risk-driven and iterative?
flashcards.back: Spiral repeats planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation in each loop. Waterfall is sequential with little return to earlier phases.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which model fits a large, high-risk project.

flashcards.back: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Used to judge whether a practice conflicts with Agile.

flashcards.back: SAMM is open and prescriptive, used to build a roadmap. BSIMM is descriptive, based on observed practices of real organisations.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Classic pair of look-alike answers.

flashcards.back: Initiation/requirements, design, development, testing/acceptance, implementation/deployment, operations and maintenance, disposal.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which phase comes first or where an activity belongs.

flashcards.back: Moving security activities such as requirements, threat modelling and testing earlier in the lifecycle, where defects are cheaper to fix.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Correct answer when a scenario asks how to reduce defects found late, such as design flaws discovered at penetration test.

flashcards.front: Rapid application development (RAD) and prototyping main risk
flashcards.back: Prototypes may be pushed into production without security design or documentation, since requirements are refined by iteration.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Appears in questions on lifecycle model weaknesses.

flashcards.front: Security activities in the disposal phase
flashcards.back: Sanitise media, archive or destroy data per retention rules, revoke access and keys, and update asset records.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Disposal is the phase people forget on the exam.

flashcards.back: A formal, machine-readable inventory of the components, versions and suppliers within a software product.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Linked to rapid identification of affected systems when a vulnerability is announced.

flashcards.back: SCA finds known-vulnerable and licence-restricted third-party components. SAST analyses the organisation's own source code for flaws.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam mixes up which tool inspects which code.

flashcards.back: A build pulls a malicious public package that shares a name with an internal one. Mitigate with private registries, scoped names, pinned versions and hashes.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Supply chain attack that appears in modern CISSP content.

flashcards.front: What to do when a secret is committed to a repository
flashcards.back: Revoke and rotate it first. Deleting the commit does not help because the secret remains in history and clones.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam wants rotation before clean-up.

flashcards.back: Integrity of the code and authenticity of the publisher, using a digital signature with the publisher's private key.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Not confidentiality, and not proof of safe code.

flashcards.front: Why separate development, test and production environments?
flashcards.back: Enforces separation of duties and ensures that only tested, approved code reaches production, with no developer access to live data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Frequent reason-for-control question.

flashcards.back: Request, impact analysis, approval, testing, scheduled implementation with a back-out plan, documentation and post-change review.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Questions ask which step is missing or comes first.

flashcards.back: SAST analyses code without running it. DAST tests a running application from outside (black box). IAST instruments a running application from inside.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Core testing distinction on the exam.

flashcards.back: Feeding malformed or random input to a program to expose crashes, hangs and memory errors. A form of dynamic testing.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Right answer when no source code is available.

flashcards.back: Re-running tests after a change to confirm that existing functionality and previous fixes still work.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam distinguishes it from acceptance, unit and fuzz testing when a fix has just been applied.

flashcards.front: Code review styles: walkthrough vs Fagan inspection
flashcards.back: A walkthrough is an informal peer review. A Fagan inspection is a formal, structured review with defined roles and entry/exit criteria.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks which is the more formal.

flashcards.back: Runtime issues, configuration problems and business logic flaws. It also produces false positives.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Justifies layered testing.

flashcards.front: Who accepts residual risk found in testing?
flashcards.back: The business or system owner, not the security manager or developer, after the risk is documented and communicated.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Manager-mindset answer in many testing scenarios.

flashcards.back: Black box: no knowledge of internals. White box: full knowledge including source. Grey box: partial knowledge.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Matches DAST and SAST to knowledge level.

flashcards.back: Source code is held by a trusted third party and released to the customer if the vendor goes out of business or fails to support the product.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Appears in vendor risk questions.

flashcards.back: EAL1 to EAL7, with higher levels meaning more rigorous testing and verification of the evaluated product.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam asks what EAL measures: assurance, not strength of features.

flashcards.back: Review independent evaluations, conduct acceptance testing, use SCA and SBOMs, and include audit rights and security terms in the contract.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Typical best answer for COTS and outsourced code.

flashcards.front: SaaS: customer retains responsibility for what?
flashcards.back: Identities and access, data classification and tenant configuration. The provider secures the application and platform.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Shared responsibility question.

flashcards.back: Provenance, maintenance activity, vulnerability history, licence terms and the ability to verify integrity of downloads.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Pre-approval scenarios expect evaluation of provenance and maintenance before any block, ban or approval.

flashcards.back: Assess the risk, present compensating controls and a migration plan to the business owner, who decides whether to accept the risk.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Manager-mindset scenario on unsupported products.

flashcards.back: Broken access control: failures to enforce what users are allowed to do, such as changing an ID to view another user's data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Recent editions rank it first.

flashcards.back: Parameterised queries (prepared statements) separating data from commands, with least-privilege database accounts.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Most common secure coding question.

flashcards.back: Contextual output encoding of untrusted data, plus input validation and content security policy.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Contrast with CSRF, which uses tokens.

flashcards.back: Anti-CSRF tokens in state-changing requests, plus SameSite cookies and re-authentication for sensitive actions.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Exam pairs the attack with its token defence.

flashcards.back: Aggregation: combining many low-sensitivity items to reveal higher-sensitivity information. Inference: deducing sensitive facts from non-sensitive data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Two attacks that look the same on the exam.

flashcards.back: Storing multiple versions of a record at different classification levels so lower-level users cannot infer the real data.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Countermeasure for inference in multilevel databases.

flashcards.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: transactions complete fully or not at all, keep data valid, do not interfere, and persist.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Database integrity question.

flashcards.back: Allow-lists accept only known-good input and are preferred. Deny-lists block known-bad input and can be bypassed. Always validate server-side.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Secure coding principle on input handling.

flashcards.back: Time-of-check to time-of-use race condition, where state changes between a security check and the use of the resource.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Named attack on the exam.

flashcards.front: Worm vs virus vs logic bomb
flashcards.back: Worm: self-replicates over networks. Virus: attaches to a host file, needs a user to run it. Logic bomb: malicious code triggered by a condition.
flashcards.whyItMatters: Common malware definitions question.
